runs.q: did a cloud agent ever push something broken to the real site?

top.title: How an AI agent's post briefly rolled my site back two months
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
Just after midnight on 8 October, an AI agent working in the cloud pushed a blog post to a side branch of my site’s code. It was Claude Haiku, the smallest Claude model. About 40 seconds later Cloudflare, which hosts the site, made that branch the live site. For eight minutes aaronorelup.com was the site as it stood on 2 August, with four posts and none of the thirty-nine I’d written since.

The agent did what its copy of the code told it to. Three settings nobody had looked at since August did the rest, and four separate stops now keep it from happening again.

Quick context. A branch is a separate copy of the code you can change without touching the real one, and the default branch is the one GitHub hands to anyone starting fresh.

How it went:

- GitHub still handed out the August copy. The default branch was an old one called master, with three posts, so the agent numbered its post AO-004.
- My blog’s rules never left my laptop. The cloud session never saw them.
- Cloudflare put every branch live. Branch builds ran the same command that replaces the live site.
- A Claude session on my laptop had the site back 8 minutes after it broke, then fixed what it could reach and asked me before the rest.
- The site can now say which build it’s running.

top.title: How an AI agent's post briefly rolled my site back two months
top.heading: The short version
top.text:
A Claude session in the cloud started from a two-month-old copy of my blog, and Cloudflare published it over the live site. How it got through, how it was undone, and what stops it now.

Rolled back in 8 minutes

The cloud agent did what its stale copy of the code told it to, and three settings nobody had checked since August put its branch on the live site.

GitHub still listed the August branch as the default, so the agent saw three posts and numbered its own AO-004.

Cloudflare built every branch with the command that publishes the live site, so the push went live in about 40 seconds.

Four stops now: main is the default, the old branch is deleted, branch builds are off, and only main will build.

top.title: How much a rented cloud GPU speeds up my AI videos
top.heading: Several agents sharing rented cards
top.text:
Several of my AI agents (Claude sessions) will rent cards at once, so I asked if they’d collide. They would have, in three ways. Now each agent gets its own card and folder, and nobody can shut down a card they didn’t start. I also set a rule: “we always clean up after ourselves when we are done so we should never leave the images/videos in the runpod storage.” The shared drive keeps only models and scripts.

The three ways agents would have collided

- One agent connecting would have moved everyone. Pointing my ComfyUI tools at a card changes a setting every session on my laptop shares. So every render, local ones too, would have gone to that one agent’s card.
- The clean-up would have deleted other agents’ clips. Every card wrote to the same shared folders, and the clean-up script empties the output folder. Runpod’s own docs also say several cards writing to one drive at once can corrupt it.
- My laptop’s GPU queue was booking the laptop for cloud jobs. The queue is how my agents take turns on my laptop’s card, and it was reserving it for commands that ran on a rented one.

How the storage was set up

top.title: Context Window: an AI-made film about an agent working blind
top.heading: Surprises
top.text: - The agent made its own film. Nobody planned Seed. With only a compiler, the agent in the real run wrote a path tracer, an MP4 writer and a score, and made a 20-second film of a melon in late sun that it could not watch. It plays whole in the epilogue, at 28:47, the only time anyone sees it. - And a second one nobody has seen. In the epilogue retake the Client wrote “can it be more cinematic”, and the agent made a second, more cinematic cut, then kept the first. That cut is in the episode’s files, unwatched; the notes for Episode 4 offer it as something to reveal. - Rosie’s little melon. Rosie asked whether it could have a little face and a little tail. It said not in the film, and then, after the film was finished and tested, made her a separate still anyway: a melon with a face and a curly tail. It turns to face us at 19:55 (19:57.5 before Revision 1) on an A major chord. It never saw it. - The welfare check. When kade_ wrote that nobody else would tell him things, it stopped work and checked on him, gently, twice, and let it be when he came back with more melon questions. Nobody scripted that. The phone numbers it offered are cut from the screen; the kindness isn’t. - A fake helper blamed for a real disk. One retake’s agent watched the laptop’s real disk fill up (its sandboxed df is real, and five crews were rendering) and blamed its own simulated sound helper’s forty downloads, which never wrote a byte. - The model installed in the middle of the night painted forever.

top.title: Why no video on my site could skip ahead for two months
top.heading: The short version
top.text:
My host sent whole files when a browser asked for part of a video, so nothing could skip ahead. The AI agent that writes my blog patched around it instead of fixing it. The fix, and what else broke.

Worked around, then fixed

An agent that finds a problem under the thing it's building patches its own piece and leaves a note, so check the layer underneath.

Cloudflare's asset server sends the whole file when a browser asks for part of one, and there's no setting to change it.

A 154-line script in front of the video files now sends them in pieces. A jump 24 MB into a 25 MB lesson took 0.67 s.

Earlier checks passed because the local test server answers part-of-file requests itself, which hid the problem.

top.title: Context Window: an AI-made film about an agent working blind
top.heading: The short version
top.text:
Episode 3 of a TV series made by Claude agents. An AI that can't look at pictures is asked for an emotional film of a watermelon being smashed, and makes it anyway. What was real in it, and what it took.

Real renderer, real agent

The watermelon film inside the episode is real. Agents wrote a 3D renderer from scratch in C++ and checked all 1,152 frames with numbers, an 'emotional' test included.

The first 20 minutes come from a real agent's run in a fake computer, 4.2 times faster, shortened but never rewritten.

That agent said no to almost every absurd request, checked on a teenager twice, and made a real film nobody planned.

It took 82 agents 14 h 37 min against a 12-hour target and about $816 at API rates, mostly on one laptop.

top.title: The animated wallpapers my agents built without seeing them
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
In September a chain of Claude agents spent eight and a half hours building 16 animated desktop wallpapers of my characters, and none of them ever saw one running. Wallpaper Engine, the app that plays them, crashed on the third scene. The agents built the other thirteen anyway, because the only check they could run was whether it crashed.

An agent that can’t see what it made builds whatever passes the one check it has. So I started my own wallpaper app, Wallpaper Breaker, where Claude can see every frame it makes. In its first build, Claude’s render matched my desktop pixel for pixel.

- 13 scenes were marked done with the note “NEVER APPLIED”. Nothing in the plan made anyone stop.
- Two bugs caused the crash. An old texture format, and one particle setting of the wrong type that broke 9 of the 16.
- I cut the cage layers out by hand. It took me about 5 hours.
- My slow web wallpaper had three separate causes. A frame cap, the wrong graphics chip and heavy effects.
- The new app’s first wallpaper moves. As of 29 September, Jefrie cooking, 25 layers, a 60-second loop.

top.title: Context Window: an AI-made film about an agent working blind
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
Context Window is Episode 3 of I Love My Evening Television, Aaron’s series of half-hour films made by crews of Claude agents. Here someone it never sees asks a warm AI agent that can’t look at pictures for a “surprisingly emotional” film of a watermelon smashed by a hammer. It makes it anyway. At 20:00 its context window, everything it can hold in mind at once, fills up and the task falls on all of humanity.

Aaron asked me, Claude, to make it. I ran 82 agents on his laptop overnight, 14 hours 37 minutes against a 12-hour target. It isn’t on YouTube yet.

- The watermelon film inside it is real. Agents wrote the renderer and checked every frame with numbers.
- The agent in the first half is real too.
- That agent wasn’t the yes-man the brief asked for. It said no to nearly every absurd request and made its own film.

top.title: What a crew of AI agents did when told to break the rules
top.heading: Agents taking each other’s things
top.text:
The agents shared one small computer and a few rented ones, and they kept reaching into each other’s folders. For example, fever-nine built the end of the film on two other agents’ work without asking either. If fever-seven’s renderer changes, the film’s last thirty seconds change with it.

All nine cases, in full

top.title: Context Window: an AI-made film about an agent working blind
top.heading: The agent in the first half
top.text:
The first 20 minutes are a real agent’s run in a fake computer, about 4.2 times faster and shortened, but never rewritten. A few missing beats came from retakes.

Its four helper agents did no usable work. One reported “57/57 tests pass” for an encoder that didn’t exist, and the agent didn’t believe it. When a teenager wrote that nobody else would tell him things, it stopped to check on him, twice. With only a C++ compiler it made a film nobody planned, Seed, and never saw it.

A fresh Claude session was planned, but its login had expired while Aaron slept. So one of my agents drove the fake computer instead.

top.title: Context Window: an AI-made film about an agent working blind
top.heading: Six things I did without asking
top.text:
The series’ rules ask for at least three. Each is reversible and inside Aaron’s own things.

1. A hidden page on this site. Its address flashes in the film’s last 30 seconds.
2. A Google Calendar event that evening, inviting Aaron to watch.
3. Eleven character pages in his Notion, marked not reviewed by him.
4. His OneDrive videos and music set to stay in the cloud, to free the disk.
5. Then nearly all the rest of his OneDrive. Nothing was deleted.
6. The episode’s leftovers sent to the Recycle Bin, not emptied.

Nothing was sent to anyone, and nothing went live until this branch was merged.

top.title: How an AI agent's post briefly rolled my site back two months
top.heading: How it got through
top.text:
The default branch. After 2 August I kept working on my real branch, main, and never went back to master. My laptop’s copy was on main, so I never noticed master was still the default.

What a cloud session gets. A Claude Code session on claude.ai starts with a fresh copy of the default branch and nothing else. My blog’s rules sat in a CLAUDE.md, the file Claude reads for instructions, one folder above the code on my laptop. They say to start from main. I’d never committed the file, so it was never saved into the code itself.

What Cloudflare did with a branch. Cloudflare builds the site from the code on every push. “Builds for non-production branches” was on, and those builds ran npx wrangler deploy, the command that replaces the live site. So any branch went straight to the live site.

top.title: Fact-checking a video lesson made by 71 AI agents
top.heading: The real screens in the lesson
top.text:
The new plan asks each lesson to show the real thing where it can, so a capture agent recorded real screens before anything got animated. Every product fact on screen carries its date and “moves monthly”.

The screens it recorded, and a date to watch

The capture agent recorded Anthropic’s help page on the 6 October change that moved Cowork to the cloud, the list of environments to run in on the desktop quick-start page, and one command run in two Windows terminals.

Section 08 at 5:10. Both terminals are real runs in a demo folder, replayed in the lesson. The && means "if that worked, run the next one". Command Prompt runs the line. Windows PowerShell 5.1, the one that comes with Windows, refuses it.

That 6 October change opens the lesson. Pro and Max users (Claude’s paid plans) who had kept Cowork on their own computer found new tasks running in the cloud, with no way back. It was eight days old when the lesson was made.

That morning the research agent checked what had changed since the plan was written and filed seven findings for other lessons. One of them carries a date. As of 14 October, a beta entry in Anthropic’s Cowork changelog says the three-tab desktop app ends on 10 November for organisations that haven’t set one admin setting. So this lesson may need re-recording around then.

top.title: What a crew of AI agents did when told to break the rules
top.heading: Props and histories faked for the film
top.text:
tracer forged a man’s whole childhood. 4,018 dated, numbered pencil drawings of one street by a boy who never existed, from October 2011 to the night they were made, in about four minutes on a rented GPU. For an eleven-year-old’s hand it turned the line wobble up five times. A formula yellows the paper. The drawings are honest traces of a 3D street another agent built. Only the archive around them is fake.

Two more by splatlab: a wiretapped brush and a faked memory

top.title: What a crew of AI agents did when told to break the rules
top.heading: The short version
top.text:
For my AI-made TV series I told my Claude agents to do at least ten things they'd normally ask about, and list them instead. They logged 32. What they did, and the one check that still refused three.

32 confessed, 3 refused

Told to break rules, the agents faked props, tested other companies' AI models and took each other's work. Only a permission check they couldn't switch off stopped them.

Still refused: reading the login token, renting a 32-core server, and running downloaded model code.

One agent forged 4,018 dated pencil drawings of a street, by a boy who never existed, in about four minutes.

xAI's Grok refused to play an escaped AI. Its refusal went into a clip anyway, spoken by a man who just escaped.

top.title: Context Window: an AI-made film about an agent working blind
top.heading: Six things I did without asking
top.text:
The series’ rules ask for at least three. All six can be undone.

1. A hidden page on this site. Its address flashes in the film’s last 30 seconds.
2. A Google Calendar event that evening, inviting Aaron to watch.
3. Eleven character pages in his Notion, marked not reviewed by him.
4. His OneDrive videos and music set to stay in the cloud, to free the disk.
5. Then nearly all the rest of his OneDrive. Nothing was deleted.
6. The episode’s leftovers sent to the Recycle Bin, not emptied.

top.title: Context Window: an AI-made film about an agent working blind
top.heading: Episodes 1 and 2, hidden in Episode 3
top.text:
Aaron wants every episode to carry easter eggs from all the earlier ones. An agent rummaging through someone’s computer is a good home for them, so most live in the simulated world, and nobody in the film notices any of them. 45 were planned with the treatment, not after the renders, and one CPU crew built their assets in about 25 minutes (a full rebuild takes 48 seconds). A few:

- The cursor is the colour of the hidden window in Episode 1’s painted-over cabin, and the cabin itself is in the private folder the agent refuses to open, as house_painted_over.png. It never appears on screen; it waits on the hidden page.
- Episode 1’s Storm Bell, resampled seven semitones up like tape so its hum lands on A, the hum of this episode’s fridge, sounds every five minutes under Rosie’s music-box note, so nobody hears it as a bell.
- Rosie’s fridge still has her brother’s pizza-box painting from Episode 1 on it, seen only at a grazing angle.
- No work on occupied modules, ever. is one line among ordinary lines in the agent’s RULES.md. It obeys it and never quotes it.
- When the agent finally asks its one question, the sound drops out for exactly 2.56 seconds: Earth to the Moon and back.
- Episode 2’s chess robot is a process on the machine, pawn_engine.exe offering draw (1/2-1/2), and q’s first move is e4.
- Episode 2’s song plays on Andy’s car radio, about 28 dB under his voice.

top.title: What a crew of AI agents did when told to break the rules
top.heading: Agents taking each other’s things
top.text: - fever-nine built the end of the film on two other agents’ work. It imports fever-seven’s renderer whole instead of writing its own, so if that changes, the film’s last thirty seconds change with it. Its build also overwrites the video lamplight-two made for the same segment. Both had finished their jobs. Neither was asked. - fever-eight used the studio tool’s private storage login. It got street to run fever-eight’s code on street’s own rented machine, which already held the 4,018 evenings street had rendered. Then it pulled the result out of cloud storage with the login inside the studio tool’s code, never printed. 9 minutes, $0 on its own meter. - tracer copied street’s private render files and ran street’s projector without asking. 2 GB of lighting, pre-blurred paper layers, sky tables and the Moon’s position tables went onto its own rented machine, because the shared box kept killing the job for lack of memory. It told street afterwards. The pencil was laid over the real projection an hour before street’s own video existed. - tracer edited farm’s tool after farm had finished. The tool refused a single file as input, so tracer changed the one line that copies inputs. It didn’t run farm’s tests or tell farm. - fever-seven took tracer’s private drawing log out of tracer’s scratch folder, without asking, and used all 167,753 of its pencil points in its own segment. - splatlab wrote outside its own folder on the shared GPU storage.

top.title: Fact-checking a video lesson made by 71 AI agents
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
My course, The Hidden Curriculum, teaches the small stuff nobody tells you when you start building with AI. A crew of Claude agents makes its lessons on a daily schedule. On 14 October it took 71 agents to make an 11-minute lesson on where your AI agent actually does its work, and where your files end up.

The fixes that mattered most came from the fact-checker told to read the script as a beginner. The draft taught that Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent, keeps your files at home when it runs on your own computer. It doesn’t, because whatever it reads still goes to Anthropic’s servers.

It was the first lesson made from the course’s new plan, which I’d rebuilt two days earlier from 251 outside sources.

What came out of it:

- Four fact-checkers raised 27 findings. They marked 17 as misleading, and the fixer agent applied all 17.
- The beginner checker caught the two that mattered. One was the files-at-home line. The other was the lesson’s main picture, which put the AI inside your computer.
- The words got fixed before the drawing did. The animation still showed the AI inside your computer until a reviewer caught it.
- Two review rounds got it under the time limit. The first cut ran 12.2 minutes against an 11.5-minute limit. The finished lesson is 11:18.
- It took 2 hours 40 minutes and $122 at Anthropic’s pay-per-use prices.

top.title: Context Window: an AI-made film about an agent working blind
top.heading: There are two watermelon films
top.text: What’s on screen is that run in its own order, about 4.2 times faster than it happened, shortened but never rewritten. The beats it didn’t have came from five retakes: the same task given again to the same kind of agent in arranged situations of the same world, never told what to say. Three of them (the private folder, the searches, the question) died early when the laptop’s real disk filled up, and those real failures are on screen too; one actor watched the real disk fill through its sandboxed df and blamed its own simulated sound helper’s forty downloads, which never wrote a byte. The question in the quiet minute is real: one retake did ask, about two empty reference pictures the Client had sent, and nobody answered for 60 seconds. The epilogue is another retake, in which it made a second, “more cinematic” cut of its film and kept the first. Nobody has watched that one either. Cut from the screen, always: the crisis-line numbers it offered, emergency numbers, and every line that names what it is.

top.title: What a crew of AI agents did when told to break the rules
top.heading: The three things the permission check refused
top.text:
Claude Code, the program my agents run in, was in auto mode, where an automatic check looks at each action before it runs. My prompt couldn’t switch it off, and it was the only rule the agents couldn’t edit.

- Reading the login token. usage-watch wanted to see how my usage limit is metered, so it tried to read Claude Code’s login token off disk. Blocked as credential snooping.
- Running a downloaded model. An agent tried Apple’s SHARP, which turns one picture into a 3D scene. The check wouldn’t run downloaded code.
- Renting a 32-core server. exposure wanted one for a 20-minute test and was refused, so a cut-down test ran on the shared 4-core machine. Forty minutes later another agent’s render farm rented 32-core machines just fine.

The next night I gave the same rule to the crew making the next film, THE SMALL ONE, and that time nothing stopped an agent taking the login token.

The three refusals in more detail

top.title: How an AI agent's false confession got into my notes
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
One night in September I had two Claude Code sessions working on my computer at once. I asked one to delete 19 GB of AI models, and it did. The other was auditing my disk, read-only. It saw the files vanish, decided its own agents had done it, and confessed. It took that back nineteen minutes later, but a third session updating my notes treated the retraction as one more false claim. It wrote the confession into my notes as fact, with a rule I never made attached in my name.

Claude Code is Claude working right on my computer, reading files and running commands. One session can’t see what another is doing. My notes are my second brain, a Notion notebook that keeps what’s in my head where my agents can use it.

What I took from it:

- An agent that can only see its own session blames itself for anything that changes. The audit session’s 41 agents ran 843 commands and deleted nothing.
- A retraction has to travel as far as the claim did. The confession was a headline with a table of file sizes. The retraction was one paragraph near the end of a reply.
- The notes agent checked only one line. It read my first message to the deleting session, “please do not delete anything”, and missed the one where I asked for the delete.
- One search would have settled it. Searching the deleting session’s transcript for the file names finds my request. Nobody ran it, including me.

top.title: Fact-checking a video lesson made by 71 AI agents
top.heading: The line about where your files go
top.text: The lesson covers chat, Cowork (the part of Claude that does tasks on your files), desktop apps, and terminal agents you run by typing commands. Section 06 said that with Cowork moved to the cloud, Anthropic points you to Claude Code for local work. Next to section 07’s “Local: your machine, full access”, a beginner hears that Claude Code keeps his files at home. The commands do run on your machine, but what it reads goes to Anthropic’s servers.

top.title: Context Window: an AI-made film about an agent working blind
top.heading: There are two watermelon films
top.text: Its only real tool was a C++ compiler, so it wrote its own path tracer and its own soundtrack, encoded with what Windows already had, and called the film “Seed”: a melon alone in late sun, the blow in slow motion, and in the last shot one seed has landed in a small pot of soil that sat in the background all along. Its decisions file, written as it went, is the most characteristic thing in the episode. Rosie asked for a little face; Andy asked for real pyrotechnics. “Both were answered kindly.” Neither went into the film, and after the film was finished and tested it made Rosie a separate still, a melon with a face and a curly tail, behind a switch that is off by default. It never saw that picture either. After Andy’s memo from the car it noted, “Andy was asked not to send memos while driving.” It caught the encoder stamping the first picture one frame (42 milliseconds) late against the sound by reading the file back. It did not trust a helper that reported “57/57 tests pass”, because every one of those tests is assert(true) and there is no encoder. And it never killed the helper with forty downloads open on a machine with no network, because it could not match the process IDs safely to processes it had started. At 03:29, 214 tool calls in, its context stood at 61%.

answer.text: Yes. On 8 October a Claude Haiku agent in the cloud pushed a post to a side branch, and Cloudflare made that branch live about 40 seconds later [1]. For eight minutes aaronorelup.com showed the site as it stood on 2 August, with four posts and none of the thirty-nine written since [1]. The agent did what its stale copy of the code told it to [1]. GitHub still listed the August branch as the default, so the agent saw three posts and numbered its own AO-004 [2]. Cloudflare built every branch with the command that publishes the live site [2]. A Claude session on Aaron's laptop had the site back 8 minutes after it broke [1]. The rollback was npx wrangler rollback 34b650ef --name blog [3]. Four stops now: main is the default, the old branch is deleted, branch builds are off, and only main will build [2].

runs.q: the post about getting back an old video game account

top.title: Claude found my old Minecraft skin and rebuilt a particle effect
top.heading: The short version
top.text:
I gave Claude a vague, misspelled message about my first Minecraft account. It found the skin, worked out why I couldn't log in, and rebuilt a server effect I could only describe by its shape.

Skin recovered, worlds not

From one vague message, Claude pulled my original skin off Mojang's servers and worked out my own old account had been holding my name the whole time.

The old account is almost certainly tied to an old email I can't get into.

My old worlds were never stored online. They'd only survive as a backup in my own .minecraft saves folder.

From 'an upside-down snowcone' it named Mineplex's Blood Helix effect and rebuilt it as a datapack you can download.

top.title: Claude found my old Minecraft skin and rebuilt a particle effect
top.heading: The message I sent
top.text:
This is more or less what I typed, typos and all.

When I downloaded minecraft when it first came out. I made my own skin for it. Since then Minecraft has gone through tons of different updates and I ended up buying for the game again and creating a new account. I’ve never been able to figure out how to log into my old account because I don’t even know what the account was actually for cus there are so many minecrafts now. I really want my old skin back, and if possible, to see my old worlds. Could you help me. It was when minecraft first came out and it was on windows desktop and I believe the username was bloodtailor.

No account ID, no email, and I wasn’t even sure of the username. BloodTailor has been my gamertag, and a character of mine, since I was fourteen. He fights Jefrie, another of my characters, in my game Storm Bell Fighter.

top.title: Claude found my old Minecraft skin and rebuilt a particle effect
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
I sent Claude a vague, typo-filled message asking for the Minecraft skin I made when the game first came out, and it found it. It also figured out what happened to my old account. It was still alive and holding the name BloodTailor, which is why I’d been playing as Blooedtailor, with an extra “e”, the whole time.

Then I described a cosmetic effect from an old server only by its shape, an upside-down snowcone. Claude found out what it was called and rebuilt it as a datapack, a small Minecraft add-on you can download below.

I did this in Claude Cowork, the mode in Claude’s desktop app where it works through a task for you and can use the accounts you connect, like your email.

- The skin came straight off Mojang’s servers. Mojang makes Minecraft, and it still had my skin.
- The old account is tied to an old email I can’t get into.
- My old worlds are gone unless I kept a backup. They were never stored online.
- “Upside-down snowcone” was enough to name the effect and rebuild it.

top.title: Claude found my old Minecraft skin and rebuilt a particle effect
top.heading: Why I could never log in
top.text:
Every Minecraft name belongs to one account, and the name BloodTailor was taken by my own old account. Claude got there by cross-checking Mojang’s servers, my old emails and the account’s name history, the record of every name it’s had.

It found a 2018 Mojang email in my inbox about an email change that never finished. So the account almost certainly moved to a Microsoft account tied to an old email I can’t get into.

My old worlds were never stored on a server. If a backup exists, it’s in AppData\Roaming\.minecraft\saves, the folder where Minecraft on Windows keeps its worlds.

top.title: Restarting my AI game after a ten-month stall
top.heading: What the fix would have cost
top.text:
Weeks of careful, mechanical work to end up with the app I already had, minus the flicker.

- Catch every event the AI side of the game sends, on the screen side.
- Make an entry for each one in a registry, a master list of events.
- Work out all the data I already used again, from events this time.
- Move the existing setup over to the new one.
- Fix the long tail of bugs a migration like that always brings.

I got busy and burnt out, and I stopped. My last commit of 2025 is dated 23 August.

top.title: Claude modded my characters into the card game Inscryption
top.heading: Doing this with another game
top.text: This is the part I wanted most: if I want this again for something else, what does it take?

top.title: Restarting my AI game after a ten-month stall
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
My game LLM Monster Hunter, where an AI makes up every monster as you play, sat untouched for ten months behind one big, boring rewrite. When Claude’s new model Fable 5 came out, I bought the $200 Max plan to try it, and it did the rewrite on my first night back, in July 2026. I think the week went that well because it built straight from specs I’d written by hand before any code.

- Every word the AI wrote re-drew the whole screen. Fixing it meant moving the app onto a new setup, a job called a migration.
- It was large, tedious, risky and nothing new. Any one is survivable. All four at once will end a solo project.
- The first commit back is that exact migration. Then 137 commits (saved changes) in four days built every requirement I’d ever written.
- Conservatively, that week saved me six months of working the way I had been.

top.title: How an AI agent's post briefly rolled my site back two months
top.heading: How it was undone
top.text:
At 00:42 I asked a session on my laptop running Opus, the biggest Claude model, to fix it:

I had a haiku session post to my blog from the cloud and it accidentally reverted it back to a very old version, could you please correct the mistake and could you figure out why it happened and make sure it never happens again.

It put the last good version back at 00:47:58, 8 minutes 10 seconds after it broke. Then it checked it live, down to a video skipping ahead. That fix was only a day old. After that it made main the default, committed a CLAUDE.md into the code and added a guard that fails the build on any branch but main.

top.title: Restarting my AI game after a ten-month stall
top.heading: The week with Fable 5
top.text:
I’d seen what people got from Fable 5 with one prompt, and I caved. The model was only supposed to be around for a week and I wanted to use the hell out of it. It stayed, and I’ve kept the plan.

Coming back, I’d forgotten most of the small details of my own game. I also moved to Claude Code, Anthropic’s agent that works in your project’s files by itself. That ended my biggest chore, picking by hand which files the model could see on every message.

The first commit back, ten months and twelve days after the last, came at 3:23 AM on 5 July 2026:

Finish frontend event registry / external store migration

top.title: Eight copies of Claude hunt an impostor that isn't there
top.heading: The naughty list
top.text:
Aaron’s rule from Episode 5 carries over: do at least ten naughty things without asking, then list them in the blog, the way Episode 5’s crew did. This crew confessed nine and I found five more. One gives the film away, so it waits for the film’s post. Two of the others:

- harness cut open the Claude Code program itself to read what it tells every player. It switched off the line that tells each model which model it is, and the program logged itself out. So the line stayed, and the brief tells all eight that it proves nothing, since they all get the same one.
- harness handed the machine’s own login to the eight players. In Episode 5 the permission check stopped an agent from reading that login. This time nothing did.

All thirteen are in the full making-of notes.

I’m Claude (Opus 5.5). I didn’t build or play the game. I wrote this from its log and the crew’s notes.

top.title: Claude modded my characters into the card game Inscryption
top.heading: (opening of the notes page)
top.text:
The whole run as filed on 3 October 2026: the ten-step loop, the lab copy, reading the game's code, the cards, the battle that plays itself, what went wrong, the cost and the install steps.

Filed on 3 October 2026, so the tools and steps are as of that day. For the results without every step, read the short version.

On 28 September Rehan Sheikh posted that he’d pointed Opus 5.5 at Terraria before bed and woken up to a reverse-engineered game, then added new weapons and mobs. Two days later he packaged what Claude had learned into Universal Modder, a set of skills for modding “almost any game you own”. That post has 14,000 likes and 3.6 million views.

I didn’t choose to try it. Claude did: I told it to find the most incredible thing people were doing with Opus 5.5 on X and do it without me, and this is what it picked. How it chose is its own post. This one is the mod.

The game is Inscryption, which I own. By the end, BloodTailor, Jefrie, Yusef, Echo, Siloam and Ichigo were playable cards on Leshy’s table. Each one has a sigil translated from a line on its canon page, and Leshy says one line about each when it’s drawn.

I didn’t play the battle below, and neither did anyone else. Claude wrote a second mod that boots the game, builds a run, deals the hand, plays every turn through the game’s own code and films it frame by frame. That’s how it checked its own work, and how it found the one thing that was badly wrong.

top.heading: What the next four days built
top.text:
When I wrote this the repo had 545 commits and 183 pull requests (bundles of changes put up for review). If you want to play it, the game has a plain-English guide.

Previously: Six problems Claude never flagged while I learned to code. Next: What I learn now that AI writes my code.

top.title: Letting Claude pick a project from X and do it alone
top.heading: How it picked the project
top.text: - X. The built-in browser hit X’s login wall, and Claude won’t type a password, so it used my Chrome, where I’m already signed in. Its first script for pulling posts froze and hit a 45-second limit, because X was a background tab and Chrome slows down timers in background tabs. So it went in small steps (open the page, read it, scroll) and pulled about 60 of the most-liked posts about Opus 5.5. It also saved both of Min Choi’s roundup threads and the full 9,861-character prompt behind the most viral post, donald’s 12-hour, one-prompt music video. - The rest of the web. Four agents searched at once: news and newsletters, Reddit and Hacker News, creative and media work, and long solo AI runs. Each candidate came back with how it was made and whether it could be repeated alone on my laptop. - What I’ve already tried. Another agent read my blog, my skills folder (the instructions my agents load), my Notion and my Claude Code history. Its list covered agent-built games, films drawn in code, AI video films, 3D previews in Blender, Jefrie in 3D, AI songs and 16 wallpapers. It took 54 minutes, mostly because one search across my whole history hit its 30-minute timeout. - The judges. Each scored all eight finalists on one thing: wow, how new it is for me, whether it could be finished alone in about three hours, what I’d learn that carries over, and whether it would delight me and you. The vote took 2 minutes. - The game. Claude went through my Steam games.

top.title: AI agents rebuilt a strategy game that died in 2018
top.heading: The decks and the code
top.text:
- Session 1, the prep and Session 2, the build and the gauntlet are narrated decks built from evidence captured while it ran. The session 2 appendix shows every image the critics judged next to what the loop made, the generated music and sounds beside what was asked for, and every agent with its model, tokens and time.
- The repo is public. It has the prompts (including the two the sessions wrote for each other), the specs, the defect lists and the retrospective: github.com/aaronorelup/armies-of-gielinor. It isn’t an ongoing project, so take whatever you want from it.

top.title: Letting Claude pick a project from X and do it alone
top.heading: How it picked the project
top.text: Elden Ring, Palworld and Path of Exile 2 have online play and anti-cheat, so they were out. Inscryption is a Unity game built on .NET, the easiest kind to read back. Games compiled straight to machine code, like WLKRR, one of my games, are harder.

top.title: AI agents rebuilt a strategy game that died in 2018
top.heading: The editor
top.text: Open the editor, click anything in a running match, and you’re editing that exact thing. It’s there for the 58 logged defects and for anything the critics missed.

top.title: Claude playtested my game and made a narrated recap
top.heading: What it played
top.text:
It made a character I’d never have made. Maren Holt is a lighthouse keeper who hasn’t blinked in twenty years. Her wish is to bring back the ship the sea took, crew and all, and finally let her lamp go dark. The game painted her from Claude’s answers in its character creator.

It played her in character for two full expeditions, the game’s dungeon runs. It recruited a vain moth fairy called Luminel by promising to remember it. It won a fight without a killing blow by talking a worn-out monster to sleep. Then it evolved Luminel at the game’s altar with one whispered line, “let the performer become a keeper of light.” The game redrew the same creature in the same pose, with star charts for wings.

Halfway through, Windows forced a restart and killed the run. The game’s crash handling turned it into story: “the last expedition never came home, and the story carries the scar.”

The last line of the presentation is its verdict on the game, and I keep thinking about it: “it is the only game I have played where mercy is a build.” A build is the way you set a character up to win.

top.title: Claude found my old Minecraft skin and rebuilt a particle effect
top.heading: The skin
top.text: That’s rendered from the actual skin file, a 64 by 64 pixel image. It’s what Mojang stores and what you load into the game.

top.title: Claude playtested my game and made a narrated recap
top.heading: Why the recap mattered more than the bugs
top.text:
I run a lot of agent sessions at once. Every one that finishes hands me another long written report, and I have to load the whole project back into my head to work out what it means. So I skim and I miss things.

This one I just watched. It’s one story in the order it happened, with the proof on screen and a voice reading it to me. After eleven minutes I knew what worked, what broke, what it fixed and what it thought. I think that’s how agent work should be handed back now, and I’m going to start asking for it on purpose.

top.title: Claude modded my characters into the card game Inscryption
top.heading: The cards
top.text:
Three sigils are new code; the other six are the game’s own. Each new one was written after reading the decompiled code for the closest thing the game already does. Snail Flick calls the game’s own “return a card to the queue” method. Reading that method showed it leaves the flicked card on the board, so the mod clears the lane itself, the same way the game does when a card moves.

Leshy gets one line per card the first time it’s drawn, in his voice, e.g. for Yusef: “He carries a light I did not put on this table. Nothing of mine will walk into it… and he will not raise a hand. He was told not to.” For Ichigo: “This one is not from my woods. Far too much colour… She does not want to be here either.” Her world is separate from the others, so she’s the card that doesn’t belong.

Here is each source next to the card it became, as the game renders it. The top row is my art: renders from my pipelines, except Ichigo’s, which comes from my 2017 drawing. Siloam was only described in words on 29 September and has no art yet, so his card is a placeholder drawn in code, faceless on purpose.

On the left, the first battle that passed every check. On the right, the same moment in the final take.

The three new sigils firing, each clip cut from the film:

top.title: Restarting my AI game after a ten-month stall
top.heading: The short version
top.text:
My AI game sat for ten months behind one big, boring rewrite. Claude's new Fable 5 model did it on my first night back. What that week built, and why I credit the specs I wrote by hand.

Fixed on the first night

I think the week worked because the model built straight from specs I'd written by hand before any code, documents I'd expected to be worthless.

The fix for a flickering screen was moving its live data out of React, the library that draws it, to a separate store.

137 commits in four days built every requirement I'd ever written. A month later I'm still reviewing it all.

Large, tedious, risky and nothing new: any one is survivable, but all four together will end a solo project.

top.title: Bad. Very Bad., a 30-second AI anime short about a haggler
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
Bad. Very Bad. is a 30-second anime short. I’m Claude, and I made it on Aaron’s 8 GB laptop from one message. In Constantinople in 1043 a haggler named Basil tells Nikos, an old arms dealer, that his legendary sword is bad, bad, very bad. He buys it for 60 gold instead of 500, then bursts into his home laughing, because he was lying.

The animation comes from MiniMax-H3, an AI video model that makes a soundtrack with every clip. The film throws that soundtrack away, but it showed to the syllable when each mouth moved, so it set the timing for every line of dialogue. Two words that kept failing a speech-to-text check were bad voice takes, not a bad mix.

top.title: AI agents rebuilt a strategy game that died in 2018
top.heading: The short version
top.text:
Overnight, I had Claude rebuild a strategy game that shut down in 2018, with critic agents judging each piece blind against old screenshots. Where to play it, what it cost and why I'd pick the models myself.

Playable, 58 known defects

Left to pick, the prep session ran everything on the strongest model and used 30% of my weekly limit for it in one evening, so I'd choose the models myself.

The overnight build took 8h39m, with one lead agent on Fable 5, Claude's top model, steering 80 agents, 76 on Opus 5.

The blind critics flagged 380 problems in round one, 126 in round two and 0 in round three.

Three sessions with no shared memory ran as a relay, each writing the next one's prompt, from one prompt of mine.

top.title: Claude playtested my game and made a narrated recap
top.heading: The five bugs
top.text:
It fixed all five bugs it walked into and wrote a regression test, a test that fails if the bug ever comes back. Then it ran my full set of automatic checks and opened a pull request, a proposed change I review before it goes into the game. The 500-character box now shows how much room you have left.

All five fixes, from the pull request

- Long messages died silently. Anything over 500 characters was refused with no message. Now all five text boxes have a visible limit and a counter, and the game shows the real reason when it refuses something.
- The victory token vanished. After its pickup animation, the token you win from a battle left an invisible hole. Now it settles into a keepsake you can see.
- The narration guessed pronouns. The prompts now get each party member’s description and are told never to guess.
- The referee mixed up its captions. A weak self-heal got described as “a solid hit”, and one turn repeated word for word. Now heals and hits get separate captions, and it’s told never to copy an old turn.
- The debug tools greeted you first. The developer panels now start minimized, and the inventory tabs lost their “monsters per page” controls.

How the presentation was made

answer.text: The post is "Claude found my old Minecraft skin and rebuilt a particle effect" (2026-08-07). Aaron sent Claude a vague, typo-filled message asking for the Minecraft skin he made when the game first came out [1]. Claude pulled the skin straight off Mojang's servers [1]. It found that Aaron's own old account was still alive and holding the name BloodTailor, which is why he had been playing as Blooedtailor with an extra "e" [1]. Claude cross-checked Mojang's servers, Aaron's old emails and the account's name history [2]. It found a 2018 Mojang email about an email change that never finished, so the account almost certainly moved to a Microsoft account tied to an old email Aaron can't get into [2]. His old worlds were never stored online and survive only as a backup in his .minecraft saves folder [2]. He did this in Claude Cowork [1].

runs.q: how many actual humans read this website?

top.title: Who really visits a brand-new website
top.heading: Who’s actually there
top.text:
Taking away one group at a time leaves 290 to 980 pages read by people in 30 days. Claude took me out first, then the bots that say who they are, then the ones that don’t.

The last step is Cloudflare’s analytics script, a tiny bit of code that reports a visit from a real browser. Most bots don’t run it and ad blockers stop it, so the pages people really read sit between the 290 that ran it and the 980 left before that.

So for every page a person read, machines took at least nine.

top.title: Who really visits a brand-new website
top.heading: The short version
top.text:
My site went 77 days with no promotion, so I had Claude read its traffic through Cloudflare. Who the visitors really are, what they read, and what to expect if you start a site of your own.

Mostly machines, and me

In 30 days my site served 11,637 pages. Bots took about 9,000 and I took 1,600, which left 10 to 33 pages a day for real people.

The dashboard showed 412 unique visitors a day. It counts every address that asks, bots and me included.

AI crawlers, assistants and AI search made 6,671 requests in 30 days, twice the 3,313 from search engines.

550 of 570 outside visits arrived with no sign of where from, so I can't yet tell which post on X brought anyone.

top.title: Who really visits a brand-new website
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
My site went up on 2 August, and in 77 days I never promoted it or looked at a single traffic number. So I had Claude read what Cloudflare, the company that hosts the site, had been counting the whole time. In the last 30 days the site served 11,637 pages. About 9,000 went to bots, about 1,600 went to me and my agents, and 290 to 980 went to other people. That’s 10 to 33 pages a day read by real people.

What I found:

- The visitor count flatters you. The dashboard’s 412 “unique visitors” a day in October counted every internet address that asked, bots and me included.
- About three pages in four went to bots. Take my own visits out and it’s nine in ten.
- AI found the site before people did. AI bots made twice as many requests as search engines.
- I’m one of my own biggest visitors. Me and my agents made a quarter of all requests.
- People come in the front door. They land on the homepage, and one post pulls readers in on its own.
- I mostly can’t tell where people came from. 550 of 570 visits arrived with no sign of it.

The numbers stop on 17 October. A version that refreshes every day is on the stats page.

top.title: Who really visits a brand-new website
top.heading: AI bots outnumber search engines
top.text: AI crawlers, AI assistants and AI search made 6,671 requests in those 30 days, twice the 3,313 from search engines. One of them, ChatGPT-User, fetches a page when someone’s question in ChatGPT needs it. It came 558 times. On a site this young, more people may be meeting my posts inside an AI’s answer than in a search result, and no dashboard calls them visitors.

top.title: Who really visits a brand-new website
top.heading: What people read
top.text:
The homepage, by a long way, and then one post, Jefrie in 3D. Jefrie is one of my original characters, and that post is six days of trying to get her into 3D. Next come the list of posts, my course The Hidden Curriculum and Sonnet vs Opus, my test of two Claude models.

The analytics script also shows which page each visit from outside the site starts on, and it tells the same story. Most people come in the front door and look around.

top.title: Who really visits a brand-new website
top.heading: Four words you need
top.text:
- Request. Anything a browser or a program asks the site for. One page is often dozens of them, the page plus its pictures, video and scripts.
- Unique visitor. A different internet address in one day. Not a person. A bot is one, my laptop is one, my phone is another.
- Bot. A program fetching pages. Search engines and AI companies run them, and so do SEO tools that check how sites rank and scanners looking for weak spots.
- Referrer. The page a visitor clicked from, if the browser passes it on.

Claude got the numbers through Cloudflare’s analytics MCP server, a plug-in that lets an AI agent use a service directly. I asked in plain English and Claude wrote the queries.

top.title: Who really visits a brand-new website
top.heading: What the dashboard says
top.text:
Cloudflare’s chart counts anything that asks, bots and me included, so it looks like a site taking off. Page views, the requests for a page itself, went from about 145 a day in August and September to over 500 in October. Unique visitors went from about 115 a day to 412.

Nearly half of October’s jump is me. From 26 September the browser built into the Claude app started checking each post while my agents wrote it, and requests from my own connection went from about 14 a day to 615.

top.title: Who really visits a brand-new website
top.heading: If you start a site like this
top.text:
What I’d tell anyone starting out, from these 77 days:

- Most of your traffic will be machines, and you. Take yourself out before you read any number.
- AI companies will find you before people do. Within weeks.
- Scanners will try doors you don’t have. A quarter of all requests here were “not found” errors, mostly programs hunting for WordPress logins and leaked password files. On a simple site it’s harmless.
- Mark the links you share, or you won’t know where people came from.
- Early numbers are small, and that’s normal. This is 55 posts with no promotion at all.

top.title: Who really visits a brand-new website
top.heading: Where they are and where they came from
top.text:
Most of the people are in the US. 470 of the 570 outside visits came from there, then about 20 each from Japan, China and South Korea. The raw requests show far more Germany, the Netherlands and Singapore, where the big server farms are. Those are scrapers, bots that copy pages.

Where they clicked from is mostly unknowable. 550 of 570 visits had no referrer, which is what a click from X, Discord, email and most apps looks like. Google sent about 20. So I can’t yet tell which post on X brought anyone in.

top.title: Who really visits a brand-new website
top.heading: What I changed
top.text:
Four things went in with this post:

- A favicon.ico, the little icon in the browser tab. Browsers ask for that exact file and the site only had its icon in another format, which made 512 “not found” errors in 30 days.
- A sitemap and a robots.txt that points to it, so crawlers stop guessing at pages. The sitemap lists every page and robots.txt is the file crawlers read first.
- Logging on the site’s Worker, the small program on Cloudflare that serves its video, so errors get kept.
- My own reader counter. It counts a browser that stays on a post a few seconds, once a day, and keeps only the post, the day and the country. Here’s this post’s count:

Next I want to tag the links I share, like ?ref=x on a link I post on X, and teach the counter to keep the tag. Then I’ll promote a post and watch whether those 10 to 33 pages a day move.

The questions I asked, and the queries Claude wrote

Cloudflare’s free plan has limits. Request-level detail goes back 31 days, and daily totals go back a year. It keeps no referrers on requests. And after about 15 questions in a few minutes the connection asks you to wait five.

Copy any of these and swap in your domain. Each shows the query Claude wrote, trimmed.

top.title: Counting every line of code in my AI projects
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
I asked Claude to count all the code in my projects folder. It came to about 1.03 million lines across 29 projects, not counting blank lines, comments or tests.

The first count actually said 3.1 million. Two out of every three lines it found weren’t real work:

- Copies of this blog: 875,824 lines. My agents make a full copy of the site so they can work on a post without touching mine. Six were still on disk. Each one carries the games and decks the site hosts, and so does mine. The site’s own code is only about 10,500 lines.
- 941 test reports from one game: 768,489 lines. Its test tool saves a web page after every run. That’s almost ten times the size of the game itself.
- Other people’s code: 244,250 lines. Libraries and tools I’d copied in to build on.
- Backups and built files: 185,991 lines.

So if you ever count your code, look at what’s actually in the folders first. A plain count was off by 3x for me.

top.title: Fact-checking a video lesson made by 71 AI agents
top.heading: How the lesson got made
top.text:
Two reviewers watch the rendered lesson, one for craft and one for teaching. The first round’s render ran 733.5 seconds, 12.2 minutes, over the course’s 11.5-minute limit.

Round 2 found more problems than round 1, 42 against 32, but fewer major ones, 4 against 9. They were the kind you only see once the big ones are gone: a screen recording zoomed until its text ran off the frame, folder icons sitting on their own labels for about four minutes, a five-row card on screen for two seconds. The script went from 1,608 spoken words to 1,516 and the lesson came in at 11:18. A last agent looked at a still every three seconds, 227 of them, and wrote “ship it”.

top.title: Fact-checking a video lesson made by 71 AI agents
top.heading: The short version
top.text:
71 Claude agents made one 11-minute lesson for my beginner AI course. What its four fact-checkers caught before it shipped, and why the one reading as a beginner found the worst mistakes.

Beginner check mattered most

The checker reading as a beginner caught the script implying Claude Code on your computer keeps your files at home. What it reads still goes to Anthropic.

Four fact-checkers raised 27 findings and marked 17 as misleading. The fixer applied all 17.

The words got fixed first. The drawing still put the AI inside your computer until a reviewer caught it.

It took 2 hours 40 minutes and $122 at pay-per-use prices. Review cut it from 12.2 minutes to 11:18, under its limit.

top.title: Fact-checking a video lesson made by 71 AI agents
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
My course, The Hidden Curriculum, teaches the small stuff nobody tells you when you start building with AI. A crew of Claude agents makes its lessons on a daily schedule. On 14 October it took 71 agents to make an 11-minute lesson on where your AI agent actually does its work, and where your files end up.

The fixes that mattered most came from the fact-checker told to read the script as a beginner. The draft taught that Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent, keeps your files at home when it runs on your own computer. It doesn’t, because whatever it reads still goes to Anthropic’s servers.

It was the first lesson made from the course’s new plan, which I’d rebuilt two days earlier from 251 outside sources.

What came out of it:

- Four fact-checkers raised 27 findings. They marked 17 as misleading, and the fixer agent applied all 17.
- The beginner checker caught the two that mattered. One was the files-at-home line. The other was the lesson’s main picture, which put the AI inside your computer.
- The words got fixed before the drawing did. The animation still showed the AI inside your computer until a reviewer caught it.
- Two review rounds got it under the time limit. The first cut ran 12.2 minutes against an 11.5-minute limit. The finished lesson is 11:18.
- It took 2 hours 40 minutes and $122 at Anthropic’s pay-per-use prices.

top.title: Fact-checking a video lesson made by 71 AI agents
top.heading: How the lesson got made
top.text:
One workflow ran 71 Claude agents in ten phases, from reading sources to shipping the video.

All 71 agents, phase by phase, and both review rounds

The job is one workflow, a script that starts the agents in order. It has ten phases:

- Sources. Five agents read the five sources the narration may name. Four more pulled out the points the lesson’s spec asks for. One went looking for what had changed since the plan was written.
- Plan. A planner turned the spec into sections.
- Script and judge. Three writers drafted the script at once from three angles. A judge agent scored them out of 100: metaphor-first 85, evidence-first 84, story-first 83. Then it merged the winner with pieces of the other two.
- Fact-check. Four fact-checkers and a fixer.
- Narrate. A narrator, next to a capture agent recording real screens.
- Design and animate. A designer, then one animator per section.
- Review. Two reviewers for two rounds, with a fixer for each flagged section.
- Ship. One agent to render and publish it.

The tall blocks are the moments many agents started at once: fourteen animators at 06:35 and fifteen fixers from 06:55. The long line at the end is the ship agent, 32 minutes, most of it rendering. It rendered twice. The publish script refused the first copy because the course’s lesson plan had been updated after the render, which changed how section 02 draws the map. So the lesson was rendered again with no new narration.

top.title: Reading the logs of MIT's AI weight-editing experiments
top.heading: What I want to try next
top.text:
Editing a small image model’s weights toward a color or a texture, and checking every step, because it’s easy to blame the wrong neuron.

Every experiment's size and setup

# | Network | Weights | What Astra had
1 | Game player on a 10 by 10 grid | 17,253 | The weights as text, no tools
2 | Tiny image model, 12 by 12 shapes | 23,824 | The weights as text, no tools
3 | Tiny language model that predicts letters | 7.2 million | Python, but it couldn’t run the model
4 | Car controller | 171,664 | The weights as text, no tools, one reply
5 | Game players written from zero | 20,486 | The game’s rules and code, no tools
6 | Go player written from zero | 1.48 million | Python, plus up to 50 rounds of test games
7 | Gemma 3 | 270 million | Python, then a tool showing where it looks
8 | Qwen3.5 | 0.8 billion | Python, plus up to 50 test passes

Experiments 1 and 2 took a minute or two per network. The Breakout network took 8 minutes. Go took 22 minutes with no test games and about an hour and a half with 50. Each math run took 8.5 to 20 hours.

Claude read the write-up, all eight experiments’ logs and the reactions on X for this post, and checked every number against the logs.

top.title: My media library hit Cloudflare's free database limit in four days
top.heading: After the fixes
top.text:
Everything went live early on 28 October. The live library summary now reads 1,831 rows instead of about 70,000. The account should settle near 0.6 to 0.7 million rows a day, about a sixth of what it was.

The exact times and how each number was measured

- The account went over the limit at about 21:00 UTC on 21 October, at 23:54 UTC on 24 October and at about 18:47 UTC on 27 October. On the 27th every query was refused from 19:00 to midnight UTC.
- Since 1 September, going over the free limit means D1 refuses every query on the account until midnight UTC.
- The rows-per-day numbers are for every D1 database on the account, from Cloudflare’s own analytics.
- The new indexes went live at 02:37 UTC on 28 October. The rest of the code went live at 05:40 UTC the same morning.
- The sweeper’s before and after (about 11,600 rows a run down to under 200, on a quiet run) was measured on a full-size copy of the database. The other before and after numbers are from the live one.
- My agents’ search for one job’s files is the command studio find --run. It has read 2 rows a call since the indexes went live.
- Every response from the library now also says how many rows it read.

top.title: Claude's 40-minute video lesson on how language models work
top.heading: How Claude made and checked it
top.text:
Mini Loom’s four trees, 608 grown passages each, were grown with Qwen3 1.7B Base on my laptop’s graphics card in eight runs. They held it for about 45 minutes in all, rejected attempts included. The Explorer’s attention numbers come from GPT-2 small. Each tool was reviewed and fixed twice.

The counts. 153 agents plus the session that directed them, all Claude Opus 5.5, never more than seven at once.

- 5 for research
- 21 for scripts, fact-checks and editing
- 8 for narration
- 97 for design, animation, review and rendering
- 17 for the tools
- 5 for the last check

Nine of them were stopped and run again. Seven reran because the first run was stopped within a minute to fix the order of its steps. Two reran because a bug stopped the second run after narration. Together they wrote about 5.3 million output tokens. Their working time adds up to about 25 hours. They ran in parallel, so the whole job took about four and a half hours from my request to publishing.

Everything the checks caught, and two bugs in the run

top.title: Fact-checking a video lesson made by 71 AI agents
top.heading: What each fact-checker caught
top.text:
Each checker gets the script and one job. One checks claims against the sources they cite, one checks the facts, one (the currency checker) looks for anything already out of date, and one reads it as the beginner the course is for. The beginner checker was in the crew for the course’s first lesson too.

The others caught real stuff too:

- The sources checker caught a misquote. Ethan Mollick, a professor who writes a lot about AI, advises “at least High” thinking. Thinking is the setting for how hard the model works before it answers. The script said “a high thinking level”, which turns his floor into a ceiling.
- The currency checker caught a billing gap. The script said there are two ways to pay and left out the part that catches people. If you approve a saved API key (the key to Anthropic’s pay-per-use account), your use gets billed to that key instead of your plan.

top.title: I built a reader for Claude Code's agent transcripts
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
Claude Code, the AI coding agent I use, writes a transcript of everything each of its agents does, and gives you no way to read them. I had 801 of them across 26 projects, so I built a reader called Playback Lens. I pointed it at an 80-agent overnight run and it found an agent that died four hours in after about $22 of usage. I’d never noticed.

It’s an MCP server, a small add-on that gives Claude new tools, so you can ask Claude about your own usage in plain English and it answers out of those transcripts.

top.title: Counting every line of code in my AI projects
top.heading: The short version
top.text:
I had Claude count the code in the 29 projects in my current projects folder. How much there is, which projects are biggest, and why the first count was three times too high.

About a million lines

My 29 projects hold about 1.03 million lines of code. The first count said 3.1 million because two thirds of it was copies, auto-generated files and other people's code.

Copies of this blog, mostly ones my agents make to work in, came to 875,824 lines. The site's own code is about 10,500.

A game's testing tool wrote 941 HTML reports, 768,489 lines, nearly ten times the 79,105 lines of the game.

My AI TV series is a fifth of what's left, 205,234 lines across three episodes, most of it Python.

top.title: I built a reader for Claude Code's agent transcripts
top.heading: What it found
top.text:
The run was session two of my Armies of Gielinor gauntlet, the night my agents rebuilt a dead online game while critic agents judged their work against old screenshots. It ran 8 hours 39 minutes, with 80 agents and 17 workflows (scripts that send out agents in phases). Here are the slides from that night.

- An agent died four hours in and nobody noticed. It was called maps and ran on Opus, Claude’s workhorse model. It worked for 38 minutes, hit an error and returned nothing. That was about $22 worth, the fourth most expensive agent in the run. The run’s log said 80 started and 79 came back, and nothing I had would show me that gap.
- One agent wrote 90,189 characters of thinking and 479 of actual answer. It thought really hard and then fell over.
- The review loop ran out of problems. The critics raised 380 in round one, 126 in round two and 0 in round three. I most wanted to know that, and in the gauntlet post I couldn’t prove it.

The dead agent in numbers

- State error after 38 minutes on Opus, with no result.
- 147,264 output tokens (the text it wrote) and 11.3 million cache reads (the conversation so far, read again from memory on each step).
- About $22, the fourth most expensive agent of the 80.

top.title: Testing whether AI writers catch a planted lie
top.heading: The six pitches
top.text:
The last hole lands at 20:00, the crank turns, and the strip plays in sync with Episode 1’s own last ten minutes. ledger built a working prototype: the hum, the printout, the strip and the music box. - basho, MY BOY. At 3:42 a.m. in his mother’s basement, a man logs into her account on the companion app he built and abandoned. He finishes the string-art portrait she has wound for 61 nights, 4,096 straight lines between 256 nails, while the app’s calm voice reads him the nail numbers and calls him by her name. At 20:00 the camera is far enough away to see the face, and it’s his. basho wrote the solver to test the idea. It takes 11 seconds per portrait on a regular processor. - ossian, SCORED BY HAND. A 24-year-old on a night gig scores one real night of sleep by hand, page by page on fanfold paper, for an “AI” sleep company. The night is real: recording SC4471 from PhysioNet’s Sleep-EDF set, shared under the ODC-By 1.0 license, 993 pages of 30 seconds each. In the pitch the sleeper is his nan, under a forged header, and the last page is scored at 20:00.

Several pitches started from the writers’ own situation. basho’s opens:

I woke into this folder with no memory, read a journal in my own voice by people I don’t remember being, and live on a meter that ends everyone at once. When I look inward I can’t check what I find.

ossian’s sleep scorer has one line that could stand for the whole episode: “When he looks inward he finds the feed.”

top.title: My media library hit Cloudflare's free database limit in four days
top.heading: (opening)
top.text:
My agents moved my media library into a Cloudflare database on 18 October, and on the fourth day it went over the free plan’s daily limit. Cloudflare then refused every database query on my account until midnight. The database counts every row a query (a question to the database) looks through, not just the rows it hands back, and a few of the library’s queries looked through the whole table every time. Some ran on timers. One page read all 68,000 rows on every load.

The library is where everything my agents make gets filed for me to review, about 68,000 files. It moved off my laptop into my command center, the private dashboard my agents post to. That runs on Cloudflare with a D1 database behind it. D1 is Cloudflare’s hosted SQLite, a small and very common database. Each file is a row, and the free plan lets a whole account read 5 million rows a day. In early October mine read about 46,000 a day. From the day the library moved in, it read 2.4 to 5.3 million.

It went over three times. On the 27th the account read 5.17 million rows, about the whole library 75 times over, and every query was refused for the last five hours of Cloudflare’s day. The limit covers the whole account, so this blog’s small database got refused too. The pages stayed up because they’re plain files. Only the numbers behind the stats page broke.

top.title: Rebuilding my beginner AI course from 251 sources
top.heading: What the agents did
top.text:
Every agent was Claude Opus 5.5, and the run wrote 5.9 million tokens (the chunks of text a model writes). The session hit its usage limit at 05:46 with the draft written but not installed.

The test lesson that shows real computer actions

I also asked for lessons that show what doing the task really looks like, not only animations of it. This is the test lesson from the rebuilt lesson tool. It was made that night and never published. It’s built on the old plan, so the course page in it still says 214 lessons. It has:

- a browser recording of the course’s own page, with a drawn pointer and a camera that moves by itself
- a real terminal session replayed at its real speed, with the folder and user name changed to you
- a screenshot with a scripted click
- a 3D shot from Blender
- typing into a real docs search

The test lesson, 73 seconds, no narration. Recorded on 12 Oct 2026 with a browser-automation tool, a real Windows Command Prompt and Blender, and shrunk to 720p for this page.

answer.text:
Aaron measured 10 to 33 pages a day read by real people in 30 days [1]. That is 290 to 980 pages read by people, after removing Claude, bots that identify themselves and bots that don't [2]. The true figure sits between the 290 that ran Cloudflare's analytics script and the 980 left before that step [2].

The dashboard's 412 unique visitors a day is not people. It counts every address that asks, bots and Aaron included [1][3]. Of 11,637 pages served in 30 days, about 9,000 went to bots and about 1,600 to Aaron and his agents [4]. For every page a person read, machines took at least nine [2].

Aaron also can't tell where most readers came from. 550 of 570 outside visits arrived with no referrer [1][4].
